description: A multidisciplinary team combining software development, data visualization, and user experience design. We are focused on transforming complex NASA open datasets into intuitive, mission-driven digital tools that solve real operational or scientific challenges

ARGUS is an onboard health-monitoring prototype for astronauts on long missions, built for the Brazilian Space Agency’s challenge. When communication delays prevent immediate support from Earth, it helps crewmembers recognize health changes and understand when to seek further review.

A shared crew console displays status summaries, and an emergency workflow demonstrates microgravity CPR guidance, logs access to patient records, and prepares a message for ground support.

details:
ARGUS is an onboard health-monitoring prototype for astronauts on long-duration missions, developed for the Brazilian Space Agency’s challenge. As crews travel farther from Earth, communication delays make immediate medical support increasingly difficult. ARGUS helps crewmembers collect health readings, understand changes, and organize information for further review without relying on a continuous connection to Earth.

Astronauts can enter heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep duration, and mood through a guided check-in or import readings from CSV and JSON files. Each indicator receives a status such as within range, needs review, critical, or unknown, accompanied by a plain-language explanation. Indicator pages display trends and reference cards explaining how to measure, why the indicator matters, how spaceflight may affect it, and when to seek additional help. A Feel vs. Data check highlights differences between a crewmember’s self-rating and their recorded measurements, while combined checks flag patterns such as short sleep alongside low mood.

ARGUS interprets readings using both mission context and personal history. Users can switch between Earth, space station, and Mars-transit environments. Published studies by Stahn and colleagues and Norsk and colleagues informed research-inspired adjustments to temperature and blood-pressure reference ranges. The adjustments change with mission day, while configured critical limits remain fixed. Applying these findings to individual reference ranges and Mars transit involves assumptions that we identify as demo parameters.

For supported indicators, ARGUS builds a rolling personal baseline using the median and median absolute deviation, reducing sensitivity to isolated unusual readings. It uses up to ten eligible readings from the previous fourteen days, requires at least five, and flags three consecutive deviations from the personal band. These are prototype settings rather than clinically established rules.

A shared crew console displays each crewmember’s summary status and check-in timing without showing their detailed readings on the crew board. A seven-day handover report brings together measurements, alerts, and check-ins in a printable summary and an exportable JSON packet. An emergency workflow demonstrates how a responder could manage a collapse, access patient records with a timestamped log, follow cited microgravity CPR guidance, and prepare information for ground support. Exporting a packet or preparing a message does not transmit it.

We evaluated the alert engine across five simulated scenarios with 100 deterministic seeds per scenario, comparing Earth reference ranges, space-adjusted ranges, and adjusted ranges with personal baselines. In the frozen-seed slow-fever scenario, Earth ranges produced thirty healthy-period false alerts, while both adjusted approaches produced none. Adding the personal baseline detected the simulated fever on day three, compared with day five for adjusted ranges alone. All three methods reached the critical alert on day seven.

A separate 2,000-run sensitivity test varied temperature noise and fever progression, with predictions committed before the evaluation code and results. Five of seven predictions were met. We publish the unsuccessful predictions and limitations: slowly developing fevers were frequently missed, and the apparent benefit over Earth ranges depends partly on the simulated healthy temperature chosen. These experiments demonstrate software behavior under controlled assumptions, not clinical accuracy.

We built ARGUS with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, and three.js, and host it on Vercel. Health-data processing runs in the browser, with readings stored locally on the device. Automated tests cover status rules, baselines, validation, storage, imports, reporting, and emergency logic.

NASA Human Research Program resources informed the mission-health context and reference cards, alongside published spaceflight studies and terrestrial health guidance. All demo readings are simulated. ARGUS is not a clinically validated medical device, and its shared-console access and browser storage are prototype features. Future work includes clinical review, evaluation with suitable human longitudinal data, secure onboard storage, and live device integration.
